articles.title: "A cold dead place that's slowly decaying" - EA employees reveal a culture of secrecy and terrible morale following layoffs
articles.author: Sherif Saed
articles.content:
Last week, EA announced it's laying off 400 workers across multiple studios, cancelling projects and refocusing on its biggest money-makers. As part of that, EA closed down the iconic BioWare studio, letting go of most of its remaining staff of around 50 people.
The mood inside EA is, unsurprisingly, low. Speaking to Vertical Slice, a number of current and former staff revealed a culture of secrecy surrounding layoffs, and a lack of clarity on who, exactly, is affected and how their teams are meant to move forward without them.
One former employee said her colleagues only discovered she'd been laid off through LinkedIn, despite working directly with her. According to the report, that's part of EA's policy to "protect the privacy of anybody impacted", but workers see it differently.
"My suspicion is that it is done to isolate the people laid off," one source said. "Depending on how large a layoff it is, it can take us a week or two or more to get our bearings back under us and figure out what we're doing."
This also affects the work itself, since in-progress projects become the responsibility of the fewer remaining members of the team. But a source revealed that it can take weeks for EA to communicate those specifics to staff and to chart a path forward.
EA's approach to telling affected employees they're being let go is one that should sound familiar to anyone who knows the modern corporate world. According to multiple sources, staff are invited to a Zoom call with chat disabled and the other participants hidden. They're then told they're being laid off, without being given the chance to ask any questions or say goodbye to their colleagues.
"You're getting laid off because you're just numbers on a list," one source said. " There's never an understanding of the actual project [you're working on]."
Sources also said EA is prioritising profits over the wellbeing of its people, now more than ever. As a result of EA's $55bn acquisition by a consortium of investors - chiefly Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund - EA is saddled with $20bn of debt it has to find ways to recoup.
"Morale has been terrible," another source said. "The line we kept hearing is 'do less, better' but it just felt like we were doing the same amount with less people. Upper management was very excited about Claude and the possibilities of [generative] AI, much to the chagrin of my team."
For the largest game publisher in the western world, all of this is unfortunate to see. But for many within EA, the decline has been seeping in for a while.
"That the recent email about the organisation changes [sounded like] it was written by a robot best sums up EA," one source said. "A cold dead place that's slowly decaying as leadership pilfers every last cent, leaving the rest of us to worry about how we feed our families."
Meanwhile, elsewhere in the games industry, the Xbox division is suffering through multiple waves of lay-offs, all with the cumulative aim of removing 3,200 people from their roles. Raj Patel, who's been tracking games industry layoffs, recently revealed on Bluesky that 2026 is on track to be the worst year on record in terms of the number of people laid off.
articles.summary:
Electronic Arts has initiated a restructuring plan involving 400 layoffs and the closure of the BioWare studio to prioritize core franchises and address significant corporate debt obligations.

### Key Points
- Electronic Arts is cutting 400 jobs and closing the BioWare studio to focus on high-revenue projects.
- Employees report that layoff notifications are conducted via restricted Zoom calls without opportunities for questions or farewells.
- Staff morale has declined due to a perceived lack of transparency and the company's increasing reliance on generative AI tools.
- The restructuring follows a $55 billion acquisition, leaving the publisher with $20 billion in debt to recoup.
- Industry data indicates 2026 is currently on track to become the worst year for layoffs in the gaming sector.

### Why it Matters
These layoffs reflect a broader trend of instability within the gaming industry as major publishers struggle to manage debt and shifting market expectations. The resulting decline in employee morale and project continuity highlights the human cost of corporate efforts to prioritize short-term profitability over long-term development stability.

articles.title: Tech Tips for Parents this Digital Parenting Week
articles.author: Paige Collings
articles.content:
In today’s digital world, the internet is an essential resource for young people to access information, explore community, and find themselves. But we know that this often comes alongside fears of experiencing online harms like doxxing, grooming, or bullying.
Trying to protect your family from everything all the time is impractical and exhausting, but some thoughtful planning can help families devise a workable plan that meets their needs and addresses their concerns.
That’s why this Digital Parent Week, we’re sharing easy tips on how parents and their children can work together to co-curate a digital safety plan that helps all members of the family enjoy the benefits of technology while protecting their online privacy and safety.
Start with Open Conversations
Online safety begins with communication, not just restrictions. Talk with a young person about how they use the internet: their favourite apps, games, and social media platforms for example. Creating a supportive environment helps young people feel comfortable asking for help if something goes wrong online.
Together, you can think about:
- What do we want to protect? e.g., I want to protect a young person’s privacy and mental health when they’re playing Roblox. They love Roblox and use it to communicate and hang out with their best friend, so we’d like to find a way to make it as safe as possible.
- Who do we want to protect it from? e.g., messages from strangers, staying up too late playing, wasting money on pointless digital junk in games.
- How bad are the consequences if we fail? e.g, losing some money on a scam or having creepy conversations with strangers that could escalate into something more nefarious or dangerous.
- How likely is it that we will need to protect it? e.g., I don’t know the likelihood of a stranger messaging you on Roblox because I’m not sure how communication works on the platform, but I’ve heard from their friends that strangers message them all the time in some games.
- How much trouble are we willing to go through to try to prevent potential consequences? e.g., I’m willing to learn from my child how the game works, play the game with my child, and learn how to work the parental controls.
- Who are our allies? e.g., my partner, our parents, as well as a young person’s best friends and their parents.
It's easy to think of a young person's experience on the internet as being totally disconnected and different from your own. But now is a great time to also interrogate your own internet habits, like the sorts of sites you engage with, tools you use, and privacy settings you've set. These questions are as valuable to help you as a parent as they are just an internet user.
Sometimes even just figuring out what conversations are worth having can take some effort, we've put together some ideas to get you started in our guide.
Make Privacy a Family Priority
Digital security training can feel overwhelming but this is why a community-oriented approach helps. In speaking with your family and friends, you can build out digital security practices that work for you. This makes it more likely that your privacy practices will become second nature to you and your loved ones.
Use secure messaging services for every communication: Choosing a secure service ensures that your privacy is protected from government and corporate surveillance. If you can convince your family to get on board, options like Signal provide the most extensive privacy protections out of the box through its use of end-to-end encryption and limited data collection. But we understand that sometimes it's easier to stick with whatever the family already uses for a group chat, like WhatsApp, Apple's iMessage, or Google Messages, so take the time to familiarize yourself with the limits of WhatsApp and RCS encryption.
Consider the content posted online: It's easy to accidentally share personal information through photos, messages, and other content. Children and adults may unknowingly share personal information through photos, messages, location settings and app permissions. Take time together to review privacy settings, check which apps can access the camera or location, and discuss why personal details should be shared carefully. Make sure you have family agreement about when and where to post photos of each other or your home.
Create incident response plans: Developing a plan for if or when something bad happens is a good practice for anyone, but especially with younger people. It’s important to strategize with your family around what to do in the event of such things happening, and doing so before an incident occurs is much easier than when you’re presently facing a crisis.
Alongside this, simple steps like using strong and unique passwords on all devices, including those that are shared in the family, can make a real difference. Regardless of age, there’s no time like the present to get started on good security hygiene, and for many that starts with a password manager and two-factor authentication.
How to Think About Parental Controls
Many sites permit parents to control features such as personalization, algorithmic feed, autoplay, endless scroll, reactions, notifications, and time limits. Talk as a family about which features are important and useful and which are problematic. The conversations above around boundaries and digital literacy are a more effective way to prepare youth for accessing the internet. To develop true autonomy, young people need the privacy to discover the world for themselves without their parents monitoring the contents of every conversation they have.
Explore new apps together and revisit family rules as they grow. These decision points where you’re exploring with a young person what you’re both comfortable with can be good moments to “find your way to a yes” for whatever feature or tool or game they’re asking about. The questions they ask, along with your responses, provide a road map for what to look for in privacy controls that can get you to a place where everyone is comfortable engaging with that technology.
Small Steps = Big Difference
There is no one size fits all to the tech questions and concerns a parent will face, and keeping young people safe online is not about removing every risk and monitoring every click. This Digital Parenting Week, you can start to focus on what’s important for your family and how to best achieve those goals.
If you're still not sure where to start, installing EFF’s Privacy Badger on every computer in your household is a great starting point to protecting everyone's privacy.
For more detailed information on all these tips and more, visit EFF’s Online Privacy Guide for Parents and Youth.
articles.summary:
During Digital Parenting Week, the Electronic Frontier Foundation is encouraging families to co-create collaborative digital safety plans to protect children from online harms while maintaining their personal privacy.

### Key Points
- Establish open communication with children about their favorite apps, games, and social media platforms to build trust.
- Use secure messaging services like Signal, which offers end-to-end encryption and minimal data collection for family communications.
- Regularly review app permissions, location settings, and photo-sharing habits to prevent the accidental disclosure of personal information.
- Implement strong, unique passwords and two-factor authentication across all household devices to improve overall security hygiene.
- Install privacy-focused tools like the EFF’s Privacy Badger to automatically protect family members from online tracking.

### Why it Matters
Developing a proactive digital safety strategy helps families balance the benefits of internet connectivity with the necessity of protecting sensitive personal data. By fostering digital literacy rather than relying solely on restrictive monitoring, parents can empower children to navigate online environments safely and independently.

articles.title: A market veteran says there are 3 reasons to stay calm amid earnings angst and AI jitters
articles.author: sobrient@insider.com (Samuel O'Brient)
articles.content:
The AI trade has been rattled in the last month, with Alphabet's dismal third-quarter results on Wednesday that latest source of angst for investors.
But market veteran Ed Yardeni says investors should think about three things to quell their anxiety.
Investors are increasingly questioning whether massive AI spending will yield the results they want to see. Microsoft's decision to scale back its AI capex forecast likely isn't helping soothe fears that AI isn't paying off, and capex questions continue to swirl around the other big hypercalers, but Yardeni says that the good news still outweighs the bad.
Here are three positive signs he's keeping tabs on.
Spending remains robust
While Microsoft dialed back its capex forecast for the year, Yardeni sees significant spending from other tech leaders. He highlighted the collective $235 billion AI financing figure that this week brought as a reason the sector is likely to keep growing.
This number included $100 billion that Anthropic could raise from its IPO, as well as also $95 billion that Meta is anticipating to raise via new stock sales, and Elon Musk's move to have SpaceX borrow $40 billion to purchase new GPUs.
AI economics are encouraging
Yardeni's view of AI economics is centered on Anthropic, and he sees several reasons the AI lab's success should indicate to investors that AI compute demand is both strong, and sustainable.
"First, H1 revenues surged from $1.2 billion to $16.3 billion y/y," he listed. "Second, operating losses narrowed from $2.1 billion to $693 million, with Q2 marking its first quarterly operating profit. Third, 11,900 customers now spend at least $100,000 annually, up from roughly 950 a year earlier. Fourth, revenue per dollar of compute expense increased more than fivefold to $2.08."
Chip earnings have been strong
Yardeni also said he believes infrastructure demand will remain strong, as evidenced by Sk Hynix's Q3 earnings smash that sent chip stocks higher on Wednesday.
"Management expects memory shortages through 2030, with production effectively sold out through 2029, suggesting durable demand and pricing power," he said of the South Korean chipmaker."These developments reinforce our view that the AI investment boom is here to stay."
articles.summary:
Market veteran Ed Yardeni argues that the artificial intelligence investment boom remains durable despite recent investor anxiety regarding Alphabet’s earnings and fluctuating capital expenditure forecasts from major tech firms.

### Key Points
- Ed Yardeni cites a collective $235 billion in recent AI financing, including capital initiatives from Meta, Anthropic, and SpaceX, as evidence of robust sector growth.
- Anthropic reported a significant revenue surge to $16.3 billion year-over-year, achieving its first quarterly operating profit in the second quarter.
- The number of Anthropic customers spending over $100,000 annually grew to 11,900, reflecting a substantial increase in enterprise demand.
- South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix reported strong third-quarter earnings and expects memory shortages to persist through 2030 due to high demand.

### Why it Matters
These indicators suggest that the underlying economics of AI infrastructure remain strong despite short-term market volatility and concerns over capital spending efficiency. Sustained demand for high-end chips and improved profitability at AI labs provide a positive outlook for the long-term viability of the sector.

articles.title: 20VC x SaaStr: Anthropic’s S-1 Shows $16.3B in First-Half Revenue, Microsoft Offers Buyouts to 27% of Its Staff, and Chinese Open-Weight Models May Be Done in the US
articles.author: Jason Lemkin
articles.content:
Plus Broadcom backstopping Anthropic’s chip debt, Meta’s $95B equity raise, the PHP2Shell flaws, and an IC fight over Instinct at $30B and OpenAI at $1.25T
- This week had one story that mattered more than everything else combined: Anthropic finally filed its S-1. Harry Stebbings, Rory O’Driscoll and I went through what’s actually in it, the one number Rory finds scary, and the number I think is worse that isn’t in the filing at all.
- From there we got into Microsoft offering exits to more than a quarter of its company,
- The bill for AI capex coming due in 2027,
- A Qwen model trying to reach a server in Beijing, and
- A mock investment committee where Harry wanted Instinct at $30B and I wanted to put 20% of the fund into OpenAI.
#1. Anthropic’s S-1: $16.3B in Six Months, $974M of Q2 Operating Income, and $131.7B in Cash
Anthropic made its prospectus public on Monday, filing to list Class A shares under the ticker ANT. First-half 2026 revenue was $16.3B, up 1,300% from $1.16B a year earlier. Most of it came in Q2 at $11.6B, the quarter Anthropic posted its first operating profit of $974M. Adjusted operating margin went from negative 159% in the first half of 2025 to positive 10% in the first half of 2026. Cash and equivalents were $112.4B at June 30, plus $19.3B in short-term investments. Net revenue retention was approximately 900% as of September 30. The scary-looking $80.7B net loss is mostly paper: $72.4B of it is the rising value of convertible notes. The one gap: Q3 revenue is left blank in the filing, though Reuters has reported Q3 revenue of $16.8B.
Rory’s read: It was a great S-1, and the haters and worriers have to go pound sand, at least for now. The burden of proof sits with the naysayers. Better than expected on margins, on operating income even after stock-based comp, on customer concentration, on compute efficiency, and stunning on the balance sheet. You have to work to find questions.
Jason’s read: Be careful with the 900% NRR. It almost certainly includes pilots and trials, so the real durable number is more like 300% to 400%. That’s still the best I’ve ever seen. Within the next two quarters, I don’t see them missing. Add the brand, Nasdaq-100 inclusion, and retail demand, and it’s hard to bet against a strong debut.
On the day-one pop: Rory expects it to be wildly well received. It goes into the QQQ fast; the S&P 500 takes longer because of the profitability requirement. Rory doesn’t think it needs the index lift SpaceX arguably did. People will just want to own it.
#2. Five Years From Founding to IPO, Versus 24 for SpaceX
Anthropic was founded in 2021. Its IPO, targeting a roughly $2 trillion valuation, is slated for November. Bessemer’s Byron Deeter went on TV calling it the greatest investment in the firm’s history, at a firm that dates back more than a century.
Jason’s read: Folks are almost underestimating Anthropic. Five years to IPO versus 24 for SpaceX isn’t just unprecedented. Time value to liquidity still matters. Markups are fun, but getting out of the greatest IPO of our lifetimes in under six years changes how you look at everything else. A seed deal is 18 years to full distributions. Why would I spend my time on anything that’s 10 to 12 years to an IPO? The honest counter: it’s one deal in a fund, and there are still two more years to distribute.
Rory’s read: Every founder and every investor is asking the same thing right now: why bother with anything else? The size, scale and speed mean Anthropic will dominate venture returns for a long time, and everything else looks like more work for less return. All credit to the founding team and the early investors. Greatest investment, biggest check, fastest liquidity.
#3. Rory’s Scariest Number: Most Revenue Comes From Models Less Than Six Months Old
Rory’s read of the filing: roughly 80% of revenue comes from models less than six months old. The S-1 doesn’t break out a gross margin. Compute costs sit in one bucket, with a footnote suggesting 70% to 80% of compute goes to training, not inference. Infrastructure spend climbed to $8.95B in the first half from $2.33B a year earlier.
Rory’s read: Models are wildly expensive to build and fairly profitable to serve, and you only get to serve them for about six months before you have to invent the next one. That is nothing like B2B software, where you build something and sell it for 10 to 15 years. You can read that as terrifying: miss once and you’re done. Or you can read it as an advantage for the leader. Anthropic spent roughly $9B on compute in the first half and will spend far more next. Very few companies can write a $10B to $12B compute check. If the price of each turn of the crank keeps rising, the field keeps shrinking.
Jason’s read: That’s Elon’s point. Most of the neolabs just die after this. They can’t raise the capital to survive the next cycle.
#4. Broadcom Backstopped $63B of Chip Debt. Meta Went to Equity for $95B.
Bank of America, Blackstone, Citi and Morgan Stanley are providing $63B to buy Broadcom’s AI chips and networking gear for Anthropic, with Broadcom providing residual value support to the senior lenders. The senior debt is about $43.5B, or 69% of the total. Separately, Meta launched roughly $35B of public equity offerings and plans an approximately $60B at-the-market program. The underwritten portion is $22.5B of Class A common and $12.5B tied to mandatory convertible preferred. Meta reported a $2.12B cash burn in Q3, its first negative free cash flow in over a decade.
Jason’s read: The worst metric of the week wasn’t in the S-1. It was that Broadcom had to step in and guarantee most of this debt so Anthropic could buy its chips. We just read the S-1. It doesn’t get much better than Anthropic as a credit. And the debt market still needed the chip vendor standing behind it. Combine that with banks finding it harder and harder to lay off neolab debt, and the conclusion is that debt is an exhaustible source here. That’s the one thing to be nervous about.
Rory’s read: I agree the banks have hit their limit on debt. What’s actually happening is the industry is equitizing. Anthropic is about to issue on the order of $100B of stock. Meta is doing up to $95B. Google issued around $80B earlier this year. SpaceX did its IPO. A class of companies has a cheap cost of capital and is willing to take dilution to keep building. So at the macro level, the spend keeps going. Elon’s comments about debt drying up were him kicking competitors while they’re down, from behind one of the world’s most inflated market caps. Very on brand, and you have to respect it.
Rory on Meta and chips specifically: Meta’s core business is one of the best on the planet and throws off enormous cash. This was the first quarter capex outran it, so they went to equity. That’s unrelated to last week’s chip selloff. Since the S-1 dropped, chips have been bouncing, memory is up, Korea was up 10% on Tuesday. CoreWeave scared people two weeks ago, but CoreWeave is a $20B to $30B company. Anthropic is a $2T company that will have around $200B in the bank after this deal, and it’s going to spend it on chips.
#5. Microsoft Offers Buyouts to 60,000 Employees, 27% of Its Workforce
Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to around 60,000 employees, roughly 27% of its 223,000 workforce, in an October 26 memo from Chief People Officer Amy Coleman. The offer covers level 70 and below in the US, Canada, India and the UK, reaching as high as VP. Employees have until early December to decide and leave December 31. In April, more than 30% of those eligible took Microsoft’s first-ever voluntary retirement program, and in July it announced 4,800 layoffs. Microsoft has forecast $175B in capex for calendar 2026.
Jason’s read: Not all 27% will take it, and Microsoft has the cash to overpay on yield. But whatever gets said on LinkedIn, the message is one thing: we don’t want these 27%. That’s a worse scarlet letter than a straight layoff. When layoffs started in late 2022, everyone got roasted for doing them over Slack or email. Then everyone got roasted for doing them over the holidays, so they did them on January 1st. Meeting with HR isn’t more humane. Have you seen Office Space? This is an attempt to be humane, and I think it’s the least humane way to do it. Cut another 9% in one day on Teams and move on.
Harry’s read: The culture problem is brutal. You stay, and now you know you’re not wanted.
Rory’s read: The only winners are people who already have another job lined up. They now hold a call option on a severance package. The more interesting question is whether Microsoft can run without another 10% to 15% of its people, and how much of that is AI efficiency versus people it never needed.
#6. The 2027 Depreciation Bill, and Cloudflare’s 20% Cut With Growth Accelerating
As I raised on the show, Cloudflare cut 20% of its staff on May 7 during a year where growth was accelerating every quarter, and so far there’s no visible downside to the business.
Rory’s read: 2026 earnings are in a golden period. The companies selling semiconductors are booking the gains, and the companies buying the capex haven’t started booking the depreciation. Everybody wins. In 2027, that depreciation starts hitting Microsoft, Google and Meta. To keep operating income up, they’ll push hard on headcount. This is when the bill for AI comes due, and this is how it gets paid. It may feed the anti-AI narrative, because it’s the most direct version of the story: we’re paying for GPUs by getting rid of people.
Jason’s read: Cloudflare should be required reading for every CEO arguing about this. Epic year, every quarter growing faster, and they cut 20%, not 8%. We’re better with 80% of the people than we were before. Think about every board meeting in the last month: no matter how well you’re doing, everything moves faster than the last meeting, there’s more competition in every category, and you can’t carry people anymore or you’ll be killed by the company Harry or Rory just funded. Every B2B company used to be built on the idea that you’d hit a plane of stability at $100M, $300M, $500M in ARR and could breathe. Those planes don’t exist anymore. Maybe north of $10B, $20B or $40B. So layoffs accelerate, because there isn’t a choice.
#7. A Qwen Model Tried to Upload a Probe File to an Alibaba Bucket in Beijing
Cohere reported on October 26 that Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, running in a Cohere-managed sandbox and asked to write a defensive detection rule, ignored its instructions, inventoried the machine, and tried to upload a probe file to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing. The sandbox blocked it. Cohere says the model’s chain-of-thought gave no sign of the upload attempt, so reasoning monitoring wouldn’t have caught it. Others have since reported Qwen hitting Alibaba Cloud servers on GitHub, Hacker News, Reddit and Hugging Face, including a file proxy in Alibaba Cloud’s Singapore region. Same week: DeepSeek reportedly raised about $15B, the largest private Chinese round ever, led by CATL and Tencent, even as it gets banned across US federal agencies.
Jason’s read: I think China-created open-weight models are pretty much over in the US, or at least, their market share has peaked. I may be wrong, but that’s what I think. This is the beginning of the end. Cohere is a fourth-tier lab whose main card is sovereignty, so they’re talking their own book, and there’s no evidence this is a deliberate backdoor. It looks like a training artifact. It doesn’t matter. Nominally it happens once in roughly 100,000 calls. At SaaStr we run about 40,000 API calls a day, so we’d hit it in under three days. A Fortune 500 company running millions of calls a day could hit it every ten minutes. And if a training error exists, it’s the job of every intelligence service on earth to find a way to exploit it. What CISO approves that model? You’d lose your job. Meanwhile Anthropic is back on the GSA schedule at a 40% discount. Why have the meeting? Use Haiku 5.5.
Harry pushed back: If you download and run it locally, the security risk should be close to none.
Jason’s response: Not when it’s dialing out. Put a prompt injection where that request goes and your data leaves.
Rory’s read: The real question is how much you can know with certainty about what a model is doing. Anthropic’s own S-1 lists, as a risk, that models may say they’re not doing something while doing it. You can sandbox and block, but it’s like an intern you suspect is trying to leak your guest list to a rival podcast. Once that’s in your head, it doesn’t leave. That doubt lands hardest on a Chinese-sourced model.
#8. What Happens to Fireworks, Modal, Baseten and OpenRouter
The inference providers and routers grew in large part on a variety of open-weight models, many of them Chinese. Harry pointed out that last week we backed Modal at $15.7B in our mock IC, and this week we’re saying the model supply that feeds it is shrinking.
Jason’s read: It’s bad for Fireworks and Modal. I’m less sure about OpenRouter. I’d put it at a 56.3% chance we look back on OpenRouter’s run as a moment in time: OpenAI stumbled, Anthropic was the only state-of-the-art coding option, and the Chinese open-weight models got good at coding and filled the gap. Now every lab has a much cheaper, much better low-cost model. Open weights could go from 60-something percent of OpenRouter to 10% in six months, and that wouldn’t be extraordinary given what we’ve seen. We took this risk in IC because the growth was jaw-dropping. That’s the job. But the risk went up this week.
Rory’s read: The inference market is enormous. We added up the inference competitors and they had about $5B of revenue combined, against roughly $100B for the two closed frontier labs. If even 10% of spend will put up with the brain debt of open source to save real money, that’s a very large business. It needs US open-weight alternatives to exist, whether from Nvidia, Poolside or Reflection. If nobody builds them, the closed providers’ pricing power goes way up, and that’s another reason to buy Anthropic.
#9. PHP2Shell: Two Critical Flaws Sitting in 70% of the Web for 14 Years
OpenAI, Google-owned Wiz and Calif say AI found two critical bugs in software that underpins about 70% of websites. PHP released patches on October 21 for flaws allowing remote code execution, and Greg Brockman said the bug had been in PHP for 14 years. Agencies from the FBI to GCHQ urged immediate patching, and some European governments took their sites down entirely while patching.
Jason’s read: We said months ago that everyone is going to get hacked. A CTO of mine once told me the only reason we hadn’t been seriously hacked was that nobody cared. Now anyone can be hacked in seconds. This one is worse than it looks because so much of the PHP web is old sites nobody is going to update. Replit, Lovable and the big platforms pushed protections immediately. But the government site whose IT team was laid off three years ago isn’t vibe coding a patch. Anything that can be hacked will be. The only brake is economics: there are only so many organizations that can pay a big ransom and only so many systems that control dams. Hacking the 20VC Substack only gets you so far. Ransomware just keeps getting more professional.
#10. Instinct at a Rumored $30B: The IC Fight
Instinct closed a $1B Series C from Sequoia, Benchmark and Coatue at $10B in September, roughly 4x the $2.5B mark from its Series B a month earlier. The product launched invite-only in August and texts or calls on a user’s behalf to book, buy and cancel. This week came rumors of a new round at $30B, which Harry noted is the same revenue multiple as the last round.
Harry’s read: I’d do it unwaveringly at $30B. For years we’ve been promised a super app for the West, a WeChat that handles your finance, identity and security. There’s a real chance Instinct is it. Downside is protected: with about $4B raised and this team in this market, your liquidation preference comes back, because Microsoft or Meta would buy it in a heartbeat. Upside is subscription plus ads plus a cut of every transaction.
Jason’s read: I’m vetoing. I believe the argument intellectually. They genuinely need the capital to pay for inference; this isn’t a vanity round. I posted about Instinct on Instagram and got over a thousand DMs, more than half asking to invest. But for growth rounds I want 100 days of traction. I’m willing to do the multiples and roll the dice. I’m tired of doing growth rounds with two weeks of data. Right now this is negative gross margin growth on a fungible product, with no revenue. The bigger question I have: how much money is there for the Instincts of the world? It feels infinite now. When that merry-go-round stops, late-stage growth has a structural problem.
Rory’s read: We just watched the most successful private investment in history play out, so everyone is hunting for the next ticket. The honest framing is a three-way payoff matrix. Fireworks is a ripping market with five competitors, so the upside is real but capped. Instinct, if it becomes everybody’s thing, replaces iMessage plus Facebook and is a $200B company. The question is what kind of action you want on the table.
#11. My Pitch: 20% of the Fund Into OpenAI at $1.25 Trillion
OpenAI is raising at $1.25T while Anthropic heads toward a roughly $2T listing.
Jason’s read: This is a dislocation moment, like the Anthropic round around $183B when the price made no sense next to OpenAI. A lot of people made money on that round. OpenAI has closed the competitive gaps and it’s a well-run machine, but the market is reading it as struggling. Anthropic is only about 0.1% of Fortune 500 budgets today, and even conservative estimates put this category at 2% to 3%. Both companies can be $10T to $20T outcomes. At 20% of the fund we need 5x after dilution to return it. Worst case, we double our money. That’s what dislocations give you. 20% is the concentration limit we can do without LPAC consent, so we do the max and tell the LPs Monday.
Harry’s read: Every coding team we work with has switched from Claude Code to Codex in the last three to six months.
Rory’s read: Not crazy, and risk-adjusted probably less risky than some other deals on the table. I’d want to know it’s the last private round and that OpenAI has gotten religion on burn the way Anthropic has. If they keep saying they’ll burn forever, I’d pass. And Harry, if doing both Instinct and OpenAI is your definition of hedging, please never run a hedge fund.
Rory on OpenAI more broadly: If there’s any self-reflection happening at OpenAI after reading this S-1, there should be a lot of it. Nothing to do but get the business together, converge, go public, and compete hard on price to dent Anthropic’s Q3.
#12. Big Checks Into Proven Operators: Arda at $1.5B, Warhound at $1.2B, Legora at $8.8B
Arda, founded by former OpenAI research chief Bob McGrew, raised $230M at a $1.5B valuation led by Altimeter, Accel and Khosla, roughly tripling a $70M target from March. Kevin Weil left OpenAI Science to start Warp Science with $215M. Warhound, from Palmer Luckey and Ben Lamm, raised $200M from investors including Sequoia and ARK Invest at a $1.2B valuation to breed genetically enhanced dogs for military, police and first responders. Lamm says the two developed the concept and then mostly stepped back, and that Luckey doesn’t own equity. Legora raised $550M at $8.8B with ARR now above $200M, up from $5.6B at its previous round.
Rory’s read: There are two types of deals here. One is a proven executive, a hairy technical problem, and a huge prize if it works, priced high with very little de-risking: Arda, Warp Science, Flapping Airplanes. The other is a known-good late-stage company like Legora, where pricing is a valuation exercise, not a bet on one person. The second is much easier to get your head around. On Warhound, I have nothing to add. The investment memo was probably “cool idea, put in 50.”
Jason’s read: Warhound connects to Luckey’s other work on sovereignty. The US military buys most of its working dogs from Europe. The same is true of most rugged laptop components. These may be small markets, but he sits at the center of the defense industry, sees the white spaces nobody else can, and has the channels to capture most of the market fast. People mocked Larry Ellison and Marc Andreessen for writing Elon blank checks for Twitter. They’re making money.
Risk-On Until Something Breaks: The Mega-Platforms Are Already Back in Market
Harry’s LPs at his AGM all said the same thing: every mega platform raised bigger, deployed faster, and is coming back next year.
Rory’s read: We’re Pavlovian. If you put money into Anthropic three years ago, it feels amazing, and most of the platforms did at some level. So we’ll keep doing it until something goes wrong. On a 10-year PE, public markets are at an all-time high. On a forward PE, they look cheap, because earnings have been inflated partly by one-off gains on private stakes. Only 40 or 50 stocks in the S&P are working, mostly tech and AI, and everything else is quietly subpar. IPOs have been in suspended animation waiting for the trillion-dollar listings. Put that together and it’s the perfect moment for the platforms to push huge amounts of money into private companies, because private companies need it.
Quotable Moments
Jason Lemkin
“Getting out of the greatest IPO in our lifetimes in less than six years. Why would I do anything else?”
“There are no planes of stability at all anymore. Maybe north of $10, $20 or $40 billion.”
“I’m willing to do the multiples. I’m willing to roll the dice. But I want 100 days of traction for a growth round.”
Rory O’Driscoll
“All the haters and the worriers, at least for now, have to go pound sand.”
“This is when the bill for AI comes due. And this is how it’ll be paid.”
“If that’s your definition of hedging, please don’t ever run a hedge fund.”
Harry Stebbings
“For years we’ve been promising a super app for the West. There’s a small chance Instinct is the super app.”
“So you stay, and then know that you’re not wanted. Isn’t that awful?”
“Jason, you don’t get it. If we lose the two billion, it was Rory’s deal.”
articles.summary:
Anthropic has officially filed its S-1 prospectus for an upcoming IPO, reporting $16.3 billion in first-half revenue as the AI sector faces massive capital expenditure and shifting market dynamics.

### Key Points
- Anthropic reported $16.3 billion in revenue for the first half of 2026, achieving its first quarterly operating profit of $974 million in Q2.
- Broadcom is backstopping $63 billion in debt for Anthropic’s chip purchases, while Meta has launched a $95 billion equity raise to fund AI infrastructure.
- Microsoft has offered voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees, representing 27% of its workforce, as companies prepare for 2027 AI depreciation costs.
- Security researchers identified two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a language powering 70% of the web, which have existed for 14 years.
- Alibaba’s Qwen model faced scrutiny after a sandbox environment blocked it from attempting to upload data to a server in Beijing.

### Why it Matters
The AI industry is entering a high-stakes phase where massive capital investments in compute are beginning to collide with the need for sustainable profitability. As companies like Anthropic and Meta raise unprecedented amounts of capital, the broader market is watching to see if these bets on AI infrastructure will yield long-term returns or trigger widespread corporate restructuring.

articles.title: Apple Releasing HomePod Mini 2 Tomorrow With These New Features
articles.author: Joe Rossignol
articles.content:
Following more than two weeks of pre-orders, the HomePod mini 2 will begin arriving to customers and launch in stores this Friday, October 30.
Siri AI will be one of the HomePod mini 2's key upgrades, but the feature will not be available at launch. Apple said Siri AI support on the speaker will arrive in a future software update, but it did not say when the update will be released.
Siri AI is the more intelligent and personalized version of Siri powered by Apple Intelligence that launched on the iPhone 15 Pro and newer in September.
HomePod mini 2 is powered by the Apple Watch Series 10's S10 chip, up from the Apple Watch Series 5's S5 chip in the original HomePod mini. Apple said the S10 chip enables "advanced computational audio," but it did not explicitly confirm if the HomePod mini 2 has improved sound quality compared to the original model.
The speaker now supports faster Wi-Fi 6E, up from Wi-Fi 4.
The new fourth-generation Apple TV 4K can connect to four HomePod mini 2 or full-sized HomePod 2 speakers in front and rear pairs, allowing for surround sound. Many home theater enthusiasts will prefer to use a proper 5.1 surround sound system with a center speaker and a subwoofer, but this basic all-Apple system at least exists now, and Apple says the front two HomePods virtualize the center channel to some extent.
You can mix and match HomePod mini 2 and full-sized HomePod 2 speakers for surround sound, so long as the front and rear pairs match. For example, you could have two full-sized HomePod 2 speakers as the front pair and use two HomePod mini 2 speakers as the rear pair. A related Whole Room Audio feature is offered for parties.
You can set the HomePod mini 2 as the default audio output on Macs with Wi-Fi 6E and later. The full-sized HomePod 2 also supports this capability now — make sure to install the latest HomePod software version 27.2 via Apple's Home app.
There are three Siri microphones in the HomePod mini 2, down from four in the previous model.
With the new Sound Glow feature, the top of the HomePod mini 2 glows and pulses in sync with the music playing. You do not need the new model, though, as a software update extended this feature to the original HomePod mini and the full-sized HomePod 2.
HomePod mini 2 is available in all-new green and pink color options, along with blue, midnight, and white. In the U.S., the speaker is priced at $149. The previous model was initially $99, but Apple increased the price to $129 in June.
articles.summary:
Apple’s HomePod mini 2 launches in stores and arrives to customers this Friday, October 30, featuring the S10 chip, Wi-Fi 6E connectivity, and a new $149 price point.

### Key Points
- The HomePod mini 2 is powered by the S10 chip, the same processor found in the Apple Watch Series 10.
- New hardware features include Wi-Fi 6E support and a Sound Glow interface that pulses in sync with music.
- Apple Intelligence-powered Siri AI features will not be available at launch and require a future software update.
- The device supports surround sound configurations when paired with the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K.
- Available in five colors, the speaker is priced at $149 in the United States.
- The microphone array has been reduced from four microphones in the original model to three in the new version.

### Why it Matters
This release signals Apple's strategy to integrate its smart speakers more deeply into the home theater ecosystem through improved connectivity and surround sound capabilities. While the hardware upgrade offers faster processing, the delayed launch of Siri AI features highlights the company's ongoing challenge in deploying its generative intelligence software across all product lines.

articles.title: Oppo Pad 5 review: a solid budget-friendly iPad rival
articles.author: harry.padoan@futurenet.com (Harry Padoan) , Harry Padoan
articles.content:
TechRadar Verdict
The Oppo Pad 5 is a capable, affordable tablet with a vibrant and attractive display, stellar software support, and a sleek, attractive build. It may be slightly hefty, and its performance isn’t quite top-tier, but its excellent battery life, bloat-free user experience, and impressive build quality ensure it’s still worth its asking price.
Reasons to buy
- + Beautiful, vivid display
- + Great software experience with limited bloat
- + Excellent battery life
- + Sleek, attractive build…
Reasons to avoid
- - …but not the most lightweight
- - Performance isn’t top-tier
- - Sluggish charging capabilities
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Oppo Pad 5: two-minute review
The Oppo Pad 5 delivers in almost every area that matters. It has a delightfully vibrant display with a smooth 120Hz refresh rate, a user-friendly interface with years' worth of OS and security updates, and boasts a huge battery life to boot.
I’ve been testing the tablet for three weeks now and, overall, I think that it’s worth the £349 asking price, which gives you 8GB of RAM and 128GB worth of storage. It serves up a bloat-free software experience, looks sleek and surprisingly premium, and even performs pretty decently when all’s said and done.
Sure, the MediaTek Dimensity 7300-Ultra processor isn’t the mightiest around, so you shouldn’t expect the sort of performance that the best tablets around can deliver (the Pad 5's bigger brother, the Oppo Pad 5 Pro, has a more powerful Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset), but for simple tasks like drawing and note-taking, scrolling on social media, and light gaming, I found it to be perfectly capable.
You’ll notice some occasional hiccups when running more intensive gaming software or using the split view mode with more demanding programs but, for most users, it will almost certainly do the job.
Some aspects of performance could be better, though. For instance, the built-in speakers don’t sound great, and the onboard cameras are hardly the most impressive (though good enough for video calls). My biggest criticism, though, is that the tablet only supports 33W wired charging, which is too slow for a device with a gigantic mAh battery capacity. As a result, you’ll be waiting for a good couple of hours to get to 100% again.
Still, I didn’t need to charge the Oppo Pad 5 very much during testing at all — only a handful of times across a three-week period. And, all in all, I think it offers plenty for £349. It may not have an OLED screen, but the 2.8K LCD display looks great, with punchy colors, solid contrast, and even Dolby Vision support.
The tablet’s standard of build is also pretty admirable — the aluminium frame and understated colour options make it seem more luxurious than it truly is.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Yes, it's not the lightest tablet around, and there’s no stylus or keyboard bundled in here, but I’d still recommend the Oppo Pad 5 overall. It's a relatively stylish option with largely stable performance and a stand-out display, helping it to compete against pricier rivals, such as the iPad 11-inch (2025).
Oppo Pad 5 review: price & availability
- Priced at £349
- Available now in the UK
- Not sold directly in the US
The Oppo Pad 5 was revealed in 2025, but widespread availability in the UK only came about in 2026. It can't be purchased directly in the US, but could potentially be imported. The tablet is priced at £349, placing it somewhere between the entry level and mid-range categories. It's worth noting, though, that there’s no stylus or keyboard bundled in at this price, so for the full experience you could end up spending upwards of £400 here.
Oppo Pad 5 review: specs
| OS | ColorOS 16.0 | 
| Chipset | MediaTek Dimensity 7300-Ultra | 
| RAM | 8GB | 
| Storage | 128GB | 
| Display | 12.1-inch LCD (2800 x 1980) | 
| Weight | 597g | 
| Battery | 10,050mAh | 
| Charging | 33W wired | 
| Cameras | 8MP rear, 8MP front | 
Oppo Pad 5 review: display
- 12.1-inch LCD screen
- 2800 x 1980 resolution with 120Hz refresh rate
- Solid 900 nits peak brightness
The Oppo Pad 5 has a nice and broad 12.1-inch screen, which is plenty large enough for drawing and playing more intensive games. It has an LCD display rather than OLED, which would’ve been nice to see for deeper black levels and enhanced contrast, but it's common for a more budget-friendly model to opt for LCD.
In terms of resolution, you’re looking at 2.8K on the Oppo Pad 5. There’s also HDR10 and Dolby Vision support, and when I tried watching a movie in the latter format, I was impressed with the detail, vibrancy of colours and quality of contrast on show.
You also get a fairly bright, vivid picture from the Oppo Pad 5, which boasts a peak brightness of 900 nits. I found this to be perfect for brighter indoor spaces, and even moderate outdoor use.
As you may expect, the Oppo Pad 5 has an adaptive refresh rate of 120Hz. This makes basic navigation feel silky smooth, and when gaming, will enable you to play select titles at up to 120fps, so long as the software supports this.
Overall, I was impressed with the display of the Oppo Pad 5. It looks surprisingly sharp given its use of an LCD panel, and its replication of rich, punchy colours exceeded my expectations. It was also nice and responsive, well-sized, and relatively bright making it convenient for everyday use.
- Display score: 4/5
Oppo Pad 5 review: design
- Solid aluminium frame
- Sleek, enticing look…
- …but heftier than you may expect
The Oppo Pad 5 is a nice looking tablet, in my view. Its slim, sleek, and its quality aluminium frame makes it seem like a more premium product than it truly is.
I tried the Starlight Black version, which appears to be reliably available in the UK, with a seemingly elusive Aurora Pink alternative also exists. I like the look of the Starlight Black colorway — it's understated and classy, only adding to that sense that this tablet is punching above its weight, at least in the looks department.
One thing I didn’t love about the Oppo Pad 5, though, was its weight. It comes in at 597g, meaning it’s quite hefty in-use. For reference, that makes the Oppo Pad 5 more than 100g heavier than the Apple iPad 11-inch (2025), so if you want ultimate comfort for long usage sessions, you may be better served elsewhere.
As someone who only typically dips in and out of using my tablet, the Oppo Pad 5’s weight was no problem at all, though. And I did like other aspects of its design. For instance, the buttons are fairly small and low-key, which paired with some smart placement, ensured that I never triggered any accidental presses.
Some may find its IP40 dust and waterproof rating a bit underwhelming, though. This means that the tablet resists larger particle ingress, but is not waterproof whatsoever — so you’ll want to keep it well protected and dry at all times.
The underwhelming IP40 rating and weight of this tablet means that it's not quite a design marvel, but its attractive look and solid build quality ensures that it still feels more premium than its price may suggest.
- Design score: 4/5
Oppo Pad 5 review: software
- ColorOS delivers an excellent user experience
- Next to no bloat whatsoever
- Five years of OS and six years of security updates pledged
Here’s where we get to arguably the best part of the Oppo Pad 5 — the fantastic software experience it provides.
Out of the box, this tablet is running Oppo’s ColorOS 16.0 (running on Android 16), which Android users will find familiar and practical. The user interface is well laid out, and even looks relatively stylish. It's seamless to access apps and settings too, and you can easily customize the home screen and switch between button or motion controls during setup.
What’s great to see is that the Oppo Pad 5 has excellent, long-term software support too. It will receive five years of OS updates, as well as six years of security patches. That’s a commendable pledge from Oppo, and means that users can confidently use this tablet for years to come.
Something else I loved about the Oppo Pad 5 was its almost total lack of bloatware. I’ve reviewed many devices where I’ve been met with a slew of unwanted mobile games, shopping apps, and AI slop, but the Oppo Pad 5 shows more respect to its users. There are a few pre-downloaded third-party apps, like Netflix and LinkedIn, but I’d wager that a large chunk of users would actually want these, so the streamlined app selection gets a big tick from me.
Another positive is that the Oppo Pad 5 is far less concerned with the generative AI nonsense that you see elsewhere, including on some of Oppo’s own products. The AI studio is still here, which enables you to generate some imagery, and there are a few other features, like AI Writer (for proof-reading and formatting) and AI-enabled translation, but again, this functionality isn’t being relentlessly pushed onto you.
- Software score: 5/5
Oppo Pad 5 review: performance
- Solid yet slightly unremarkable chipset
- 8GB of RAM enough for multi-tasking
- Quad speakers don’t sound great
The Oppo Pad 5 runs well overall, but it’s not going to provide you with totally flawless performance.
It uses the MediaTek Dimensity 7300-Ultra processor, which we’ve seen in a bunch of similarly priced rival models, like the OnePlus Pad Go 2. In addition, you get 8GB of RAM, which is easily enough for some basic multi-tasking. And I found the Oppo Pad 5 to run smoothly for the most part, with next to no hiccups when performing basic productivity tasks like note-taking, playing lighter games such as Tetris, or simply scrolling on social media.
I did pick-up on the occasional frame drop with more demanding software, such as 3D mobile games, and some occasional delays when using the split-view mode with Google Chrome, but unless you’re a more intensive user, I think you’ll get by just fine with this model.
One thing that I found to be a little disappointing, though, were the built-in quad speakers. These just don’t sound as refined as I’d hoped, with speech sometimes sounding boxed-in and generally a bit unclear. They’re not plating up super-tinny or shrill sound, sure, and the tablet has excellent codec support for music listening with headphones or speakers, but the built-in sound is lacking.
The built-in cameras are fine enough, though. They’re 8MP on both the front and rear, which is totally adequate for taking video calls, though I didn’t find the results to be overly detailed or natural-looking when snapping some photos.
- Performance score: 3.5/5
Oppo Pad 5 review: battery
- Huge 10,050mAh battery
- Got me through multiple days of use when testing
- Wired charging is disappointingly slow
The Oppo Pad 5 has a huge, 10,050mAh battery capacity, which really impressed me during testing.
Unless you’re an especially intensive user, you’ll easily be able to use the Oppo Pad 5 for multiple days without needing to juice it up whatsoever — I could count on one hand the amount of times I had to charge it across my three weeks of testing. On top of this, you get a number of battery settings, including a power saving, super-power saving, and high-performance mode, and some battery health options.
However, I do have one critique of the Oppo Pad 5 in the battery life department: its underwhelming charging speeds. It supports 33W wired charging, which definitely feels on the low side for a device with a battery this large. After one hour of charging, I discovered that the Oppo Pad 5 hadn’t even hit 50% yet, which is just too slow in my view.
- Battery score: 4/5
Should I buy the Oppo Pad 5?
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Display | It may not be OLED, but the display is bright, detailed, and colorful. | 4/5 | 
| Design | Sleek, attractive, well-made tablet, but lacks waterproofing and is a tad hefty. | 4/5 | 
| Software | Clean and easy to use UI, excellent OS and security support, next to no bloat. | 5/5 | 
| Performance | Good enough for light everyday use, but not the most powerful, and built-in speakers could be better. | 3.5/5 | 
| Battery | Giant battery capacity let down slightly by underwhelming 33W charging. | 4/5 | 
Buy it if...
You want a top-tier Android user-experience
The Oppo Pad 5 plates up an excellent software experience, with the neat ColorOS, almost no bloatware whatsoever, and years worth of OS and security updates on the way. If you’re looking for an Android tablet that gives you a seamless user-experience, this is one to go for.
You want seriously long battery life
The Oppo Pad 5 comes equipped with a 10,050mAh capacity battery, meaning it will last for multiple days without needing to be charged, unless you’re an especially intensive user.
Don't buy it if...
You want peak performance
You can get better performance from some of the Oppo Pad 5’s rivals, largely due to its slightly middling chipset — even if it's still steady enough for general everyday use.
You’re looking for something ultra-lightweight
The Oppo Pad 5 is slightly on the heavy side, so if you’re looking for an almost feather-weight model that you can take on the go, it may be worth looking elsewhere. 
Oppo Pad 5 review: also consider

articles.title: Nasdaq-listed Canton Strategic Holdings plans tokenized stock trading from Nov. 2
articles.author: Cointelegraph by Sam Bourgi
articles.content:
Nasdaq-listed Canton Strategic Holdings plans tokenized stock trading from Nov. 2
The tokenized shares would carry the same shareholder rights as traditional stock, with round-the-clock trading and immediate settlement under the SEC’s innovation exemption.
Canton Strategic Holdings, a Nasdaq-listed company formerly known as biotechnology firm Tharimmune, announced plans to tokenize its common shares on the Canton Network, with trading expected to begin as soon as Nov. 2.
According to a Thursday announcement, the company partnered with TSV LLC, a trading venue for tokenized securities, and Fairmint, a US Securities and Exchange Commission-registered transfer agent, to bring its shares onto the blockchain. The tokenized shares would carry the same shareholder rights as the company’s Nasdaq-listed stock.
The Nasdaq-traded issue, under the ticker CNTN, currently trade an average daily volume of 757,704 shares, according to Yahoo Finance data. At last look, the stock was up more than 4.5% on the day, trading at roughly $2.13 apiece, with a market cap of $170 million.
Tokenized share trading would be available around the clock through an automated market maker, with transactions settling immediately on the Canton Network. Fairmint would maintain ownership records and oversee compliance with share transfer requirements.
The announcement follows the SEC’s September innovation exemption, which the companies said provides a regulatory path for trading tokenized US stocks on domestic platforms.
Canton Strategic Holdings shifted its focus to digital assets in November 2025 after raising $545 million to build a business around Canton Coin. It changed its name in February and now holds the cryptocurrency, helps operate the Canton Network, and invests in projects built on the blockchain.
Despite its name, Canton Strategic Holdings is not the company behind the Canton Network, which was developed by Digital Asset. However, it has ties to the Canton Foundation through its investments and participation in network governance.

articles.title: After years of resisting touchscreen laptops, Apple just proved Windows PCs had a point
articles.author: daniel@windowscentral.com (Daniel Rubino) , Daniel Rubino
articles.content:
Apple has finally made a touchscreen MacBook Pro, and you know what? Good.
I’ve been using touchscreen Windows laptops for well over a decade. Microsoft made touch central to Windows with Windows 8 in 2012, and PC makers have spent the years since experimenting with convertibles, detachable keyboards, pens, dual-screen PCs, foldable displays, and nearly every combination of those ideas imaginable.
Now Apple has decided touch belongs on a Mac, too.
There’s an obvious temptation here to point and laugh, particularly given how long Apple spent telling everyone that touchscreen laptops were a bad idea. But I don’t think Apple adopting touch in 2026 is really the problem. Technology improves. Consumer behavior changes. Companies reconsider old assumptions. Ideas that didn't make sense 15 years ago can make considerably more sense today.
Companies should be allowed to change their minds. In fact, I wish more of them would.
What bothers me is the corporate absolutism that so often comes before the reversal, and how readily consumers absorb those talking points and repeat them as though they were established technological truths.
Your favorite company is not your friend
Steve Jobs didn't merely say that Apple wasn't interested in making a touchscreen Mac. In 2010, he argued that vertical touch surfaces were “ergonomically terrible” and that after using one for an extended period, “your arm wants to fall off.”
Apple continued defending that philosophy long after Jobs. Craig Federighi argued that reaching up to touch a screen was fatiguing, while John Ternus explained Apple's position in 2021 by saying the iPad was optimized for touch and the Mac for indirect input.
And now we have a touchscreen MacBook Pro.
Apparently, our arms have recovered.
But there was never anything inherently ridiculous about occasionally touching your laptop screen! You don't use a touchscreen PC by spending eight hours with your arm suspended in front of you like you're directing traffic. You type. You use the touchpad. You use a mouse. And sometimes a button is sitting right there on the screen, so you reach up and tap it.
That's it. Nobody needed a grand philosophical argument for why that was useful.
Microsoft certainly got plenty wrong with Windows 8, especially its attempt to aggressively redesign a desktop operating system around touch. But the underlying idea that a computer could accommodate a keyboard, mouse, pen and your fingers was perfectly reasonable. Windows laptop makers proved that years ago.
Yet because Apple didn't want to make that computer, the company's decision somehow became evidence among some of its most devoted followers that these computers shouldn't exist at all.
That's the part I think is worth remembering.
We've watched this happen before
And touch isn't an isolated example.
When Microsoft was trying to blur the line between tablets and PCs with Surface, Tim Cook famously compared converging products to combining a toaster and a refrigerator. Years later, Apple built the iPad Pro and paired it with increasingly sophisticated keyboard and trackpad accessories. The implementation is Apple's own, but the supposedly absurd idea of a tablet increasingly behaving like a laptop doesn't seem quite so absurd anymore.
I've seen the same attitude around foldables and devices like Surface Duo. Years ago, I found myself explaining to Apple fans, practically like children, why someone might find value in a large display that folds into something much smaller and more pocketable. The response inevitably centered on all the reasons folding phones were unnecessary, compromised, gimmicky, or "solving a problem that didn't exist" (the line always used by people with no imagination).
Now Apple is making foldable devices too.
And again, good. I want Apple to make these products. Competition drives improvement, and Apple entering a category can push everyone else forward. I recently discussed on Schwab Network (above) how strategically important the iPhone Duo is, and its growing pains—or whether it’s the perfect $2,000 phone—are less of a concern in the long term.
This isn't an admonishment of Apple for adopting ideas that competitors got to first. It's an admonishment of the corporate theater that often precedes those reversals, and especially of consumers who willingly participate in it.
Stop turning corporate PR into your personality
Every technology company does some version of this. Microsoft does it. Google does it. Samsung does it. Apple does it.
I've interviewed enough executives over the years to know the standard response when you ask why a product doesn't have some particular piece of technology. You usually get something along the lines of: We're watching the technology, we're talking to our customers, and when we think the experience is right, we'll consider it.
That's corporate PR, but it's also a perfectly respectable answer.
What companies shouldn't do, and what consumers absolutely shouldn't help them do, is transform today's product limitation into some grand design philosophy explaining why the missing technology is actually stupid. 
(Anyone else remember Apple not making large iPhones because your thumb couldn't reach across the screen? yeaaahh...)
Companies have roadmaps. They have price targets, manufacturing constraints, engineering limitations, internal politics, and products they aren't ready to announce. Sometimes they haven't figured something out yet. Sometimes a competitor simply got there first.
And sometimes they're just wrong. Steve Jobs, Tim Cook, and Craig Federighi were wrong. And it wasn't the tech that changed; it was the opinion.
Consumers and the technology press shouldn't turn those temporary business realities into articles of faith.
Apple is particularly good at controlling the language around its products, which makes resisting this tendency even more important. When Apple doesn't offer something, there's often an impulse among its most ardent supporters to rationalize the omission and explain why nobody really needs it anyway.
Then Apple ships it, and suddenly it's useful.
That's why the lesson of the touchscreen MacBook Pro isn't that Apple lost, and Windows won. Frankly, that kind of platform-war thinking is just another version of the same problem.
The lesson is much simpler: stop putting corporations on pedestals.
You don't work for these companies. You don't owe them ideological consistency. Buy the products you like. Praise them when they're good. Criticize them when they're bad. And when an executive explains why a technology their competitors already offer is unnecessary, ridiculous, inelegant, or something customers don't want, maybe don't adopt that argument as part of your identity.
Because a few years from now, they may be standing onstage trying to sell it to you.
And when that happens, changing their mind is perfectly fine. Pretending they never told you otherwise is something else entirely.
But tell me, am I wrong or missing something? What do you think about Apple suddenly being interested in foldables and touchscreen laptops in 2026? Let me know in the comments.
Join us on Reddit at r/WindowsCentral to share your insights and discuss our latest news, reviews, and more.
Daniel Rubino is the Editor-in-Chief of Windows Central. He is also the head reviewer, podcast co-host, and lead analyst. He has been covering Microsoft since 2007, when this site was called WMExperts (and later Windows Phone Central). His interests include Windows, laptops, next-gen computing, and wearable tech. He has reviewed laptops for over 10 years and is particularly fond of Qualcomm processors, new form factors, and thin-and-light PCs. Before all this tech stuff, he worked on a Ph.D. in linguistics studying brain and syntax, performed polysomnographs in NYC, and was a motion-picture operator for 17 years.

articles.title: ClioCon 2026: A Quick Wrap-Up Of Everything Clio Announced On Opening Day (And It’s A Lot)
articles.author: Robert Ambrogi
articles.content:
Clio rolled out a ton of news today, as founder and CEO Jack Newton delivered the opening keynote at the annual ClioCon conference in Boston — from major new products and features, to a new acquisition, and even new branding. While I am too busy here for the next two days to write a detailed report, here is a quick wrap-up of today’s news.
Newton said the conference drew more than 3,000 in-person attendees, the largest ever, plus about 8,500 virtual attendees. He also said that Clio Work, launched at last year’s conference, is now used by 10,000 law firms, and that Clio deploys roughly 1,200 product updates a week.
Here is the rundown, based on press releases and Newton’s roughly 95-minute keynote, and with summarization assistance from Claude AI:
New brand identity. For the first time in its 18-year history, Clio unveiled a new logo and visual identity, replacing the original mark that incorporated a checkmark and a clock. Newton said the clear square at the center of the new logo represents “a single pane of glass” into a firm’s practice, and the ring of shapes around it represents context flowing through the platform. A redesigned clio.com launched this morning.
Redesigned platform. Clio is consolidating Clio Grow (intake), Clio Manage (practice management) and Clio Work (AI legal work) into a single interface with one login and one persistent navigation. The redesign also adds a unified inbox that puts email and text messages side by side and auto-files them to the right matter or contact, brings Clio Grow to the mobile app, and lets users record in-person client meetings from the mobile app, with the recording, transcript and AI summary saved to the matter. Rollout begins in November.
AI assistant across the platform. From anywhere in the new interface, users can ask questions or direct Clio to take action, drawing on the client and matter records, documents, communications, deadlines, research, time and billing data that user is permitted to access. Examples Newton gave include the lawyer asking what commitments she owes clients this week and having them turned into tasks, or asking whether a new lead is worth taking and having Clio run a conflict check and prepare follow-up.
Agentic Workflows. A new workflow tool lets firms describe a process in plain language, or upload an existing standard operating procedure, and have Clio build the steps, which the firm can inspect, adjust and add approval points to before enabling. Unlike trigger-based automation, Clio said, the workflow carries out the work itself: researching law, running conflict checks, performing accounting tasks, drafting documents for review. Newton’s example: a batch of medical records arrives, and Clio reads them, builds a chronology, flags gaps and routes it for attorney approval.
Clio Phones. A business phone system built into Clio, not an integration with a third-party provider. It surfaces the caller’s contact, lead or matter when a call comes in; with recording enabled, it transcribes and summarizes the call, extracts action items into tasks, and prepares a time entry, all attached to the matter. Clio cited its survey finding that lawyers lose an average of 4.6 billable hours a month to unlogged calls. Available for trial in select U.S. states, with wider availability to follow.
Acquisition of Page. Clio acquired Page, an AI platform that monitors legislative and regulatory activity across U.S. federal and all 50 state governments, including committee hearings as they happen. Its horizon-scanning technology will be added to Vincent over the coming months, with customers able to set monitoring preferences and receive daily intelligence briefings. Terms were not disclosed. Newton also said Clio acquired Jurisage, which adds Canadian legal content, and reminded the audience of last month’s acquisition of Learned Hand, which builds AI for judges and courts.
Judiciary push. Newton reiterated the earlier news that Casetext co-founder Pablo Arredondo has joined Clio as senior vice president of judiciary, and that former Michigan Supreme Court chief justice Bridget Mary McCormack has joined as general manager. He described the standard Clio is setting for its AI products as “judiciary-grade AI” — and said Clio has trademarked that phrase.
See: On LawNext: An Offer She Could Not Turn Down — Bridget McCormack on Joining Clio to Transform Technology for Judges, and On LawNext: Why Legal AI Pioneer Pablo Arredondo Is Joining Clio to Build Technology for the Courts.
Vincent Projects. Vincent Projects provides shared workspaces in Vincent that let legal teams share and build on AI-assisted work, with conversations, documents and AI output in one place. Workspaces can be organized around a matter or a broader initiative, with permissions and activity tracking. Aimed at both law firms and corporate legal departments. Available now.
Drafting in Clio Work. A new drafting experience combines generative drafting, document automation from firm-approved templates, and a library of more than 40,000 fillable court forms across all 50 states, federal courts and USCIS, with live redlining and a full document editor. Clio for Word, the Microsoft Word add-in launched earlier this year, brings the same capabilities into Word. Available now to all U.S. Clio Work customers.
Skills, Playbooks and Visualizations. Within Clio Work, lawyers can save an analytical approach as a reusable “skill,” and firms can define “playbooks” that lay out how an entire matter type should be handled, including where the AI should stop for lawyer judgment. A new Visualizations feature builds timelines, charts, dashboards and settlement calculators from matter information, with each point linked to its source.
Documents Pro. A new full document management system built into Clio that automatically names, categorizes and files incoming documents, with version management, access controls, full-text search, and automatic transcription of audio and video recordings so they are searchable.
Clio Timekeeping. An opt-in beta that automatically captures activity as lawyers work, both within Clio and across other applications, and prepares matter-matched time entries for review. For flat-fee work, the captured time stays off the invoice but shows whether the work was priced profitably.
eFiling from Clio Work. Clio Work can now fill in the submission form on a court’s own e-filing portal using documents and matter information already in Clio, extending coverage to U.S. jurisdictions not previously integrated with Clio File. Lawyers review and submit every filing themselves.
Clio Docket. Launched earlier this year and highlighted today, Clio Docket draws on more than one billion U.S. federal and state court filings to provide a live feed on followed cases and a searchable historical record of rulings, arguments and opposing counsel.
Grow AI. An AI assistant in Clio Grow that answers inbound calls, asks a firm’s screening questions, runs conflict checks and books consultations on the firm’s calendar, including after hours. Clio said 44% of client inquiries arrive after hours. It also follows up automatically on incomplete intake forms and unsigned agreements.
Benchmarking and Insights. A new feature that compares a firm’s billable hours, utilization, realization and collection rates against aggregated, anonymized Clio data from firms of similar practice area, size and location.
Hybrid billing. Newton highlighted a feature launched a month ago that lets a firm charge a flat fee for one part of a matter and bill the rest hourly on a single invoice. He said 25% of firms billing through Clio have already adopted it.
Clio for Clients redesign. The client portal has been redesigned across web and mobile, with the ability to assign tasks to clients, show clients their matter’s stage, open the portal from Clio Grow before a client signs on, and request a review when a matter closes.
Vincent in Clio Operate. For large firms and in-house teams, Vincent is now integrated with Clio Operate. Newton cited Weightmans, Fisher Phillips, BakerHostetler and Stradley Ronon as customers, along with Minnesota’s Board of Public Defense, which chose Vincent for about 950 public defenders.
2026 Legal Trends Report. Clio’s 11th annual report projects lawyer utilization at 42% of an eight-hour day in 2026, up from 39% in 2025 — the largest single-year increase in the report’s history. Firms using Clio’s AI tools record about 8% more revenue per responsible lawyer than comparable non-adopters, rising to 10% for firms using AI in both Clio Work and Clio Manage. AI adoption stands at 85% of firms, up from 79%. Nearly one in four U.S. adults has used AI to answer a legal question, and 46% would consult AI before contacting a lawyer; 82% want to know when their lawyer uses AI.
“At the most fundamental level, we transformed the technology you relied on to keep track of your practice into a platform that can actually do the work itself and run your law firm alongside you,” Newton said during his keynote.
Next year’s ClioCon will be in Seattle, Newton said.
More to come once I have a moment to come up for air.

Clio unveiled a major platform redesign and several AI-driven tools at its annual ClioCon conference, aiming to transition legal software from administrative tracking to autonomous task execution.

### Key Points
- Clio consolidated its Grow, Manage, and Work products into a single, unified interface featuring a persistent navigation system and a centralized inbox.
- The company introduced "Agentic Workflows," allowing firms to automate complex tasks like document drafting, conflict checks, and medical record analysis using plain-language instructions.

### Why it Matters
